questions.question_text: Which phenomenon is commonly used in a functional MRI scan to make inferences about brain activity?

options.text: Fast low angle shot radiofrequency pulses (FLASH)

questions.explanation:
The goal of fMRI is to visualise brain activity and so spatial resolution is sacrificed to the benefit of temporal resolution. fMRI is not at sufficient temporal resolution to directly measure the neuronal signal and so it measures an indirect index of neuronal activity – the blood oxygen-level dependent (BOLD) contrast. The principle behind BOLD is that an active population of neurons will receive more fresh, oxygen-risk blood flow than non-active neurons. It is this variation between the magnetic signal of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood in the brain that constitutes the basis for the fMRI signal.
Ref: Martinelli C, Shergill SS. Everything you wanted to know about neuroimaging and psychiatry, but were afraid to ask. BJPsych Advances. 2015 Jul;21(4):251-60.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a good practice while using interpreters?

options.text: Ask the interpreter about patient's guarded nature while answering
Offering to debrief the interpreter if needed after interpretation
Encourage interpretation and then translation of mental status examination
Brief the interpreter before seeing the patient
Sticking to the same interpreter for a single case

correct_answer.text: Encourage interpretation and then translation of mental status examination

correct_answers.text: Encourage interpretation and then translation of mental status examination

questions.explanation: When using an interpreter, explain the need for providing a literal translation of a patient's account. If the interpreter provides a 'summarised translation' or 'interpretations' of the reported account, several salient aspects may be missed during a Mental Status Examination.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is an advantage of open ended questions over closed questions?

options.text: Answers to open questions are highly time-saving
Answers to open questions are doctor-directed
Answers to open questions are highly reliable
Answers to open questions are less precise
Answers to open questions are more informative

correct_answer.text: Answers to open questions are more informative

correct_answers.text: Answers to open questions are more informative

questions.explanation:
An open question does not suggest the possible answer, while a close question expects a limited range of replies. Beginning an interview with open questions can provide informative answers, before turning to more closed questions to clarify details or factual points.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 50.

questions.question_text: In which of the following situations is closed questioning a useful technique?

options.text: At the later part of interview
To rule out less likely symptoms

questions.explanation: Closed questions are better avoided in early parts of interview as they can produce prescribed answers lacking in detail. Close questions must be avoided in highly suggestible patients. A good technique is to start with open; move to closed by the end of the interview. Useful to rule out less likely symptoms. The answers for closed questions can only be 'yes' or 'no', in most occasions. When clubbed with non-facilitative gestures, can be detrimental to interview process. Stating a presumption followed by tags can be very directive.

questions.question_text: All of the following techniques are useful in facilitating disclosure EXCEPT
questions.explanation: Suggestive questions have answers that are contained in the question itself. This misleads both the patient and the doctor. The patient is often left with little choice than to agree with the suggestion.

questions.question_text: The most common opportunistic infection in a patient with AIDS is
questions.explanation: Toxoplasmosis is common in AIDS. Brain imaging shows multiple ring-shaped contrast enhancing lesions. MRI is considered superior to CT scanning with IV contrast material with either modality improving the diagnostic yield and accuracy.

questions.question_text: An anorexic patient repeatedly vomits. Which of the following is a possible complication?
questions.explanation:
In anorexia nervosa, hypokalemic/hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis can result from vomiting (loss of gastric acid). Metabolic acidosis can result from laxative abuse.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 414.

questions.question_text: Which of the following SPECT finding is seen in Alzheimer disease?

options.text: Multiple zones of ischaemia in left hemisphere

questions.explanation:
In Alzheimer disease, SPECT shows temporal and posterior parietal hypoperfusion.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 157.

questions.question_text: Wernicke encephalopathy is directly caused by a deficiency of
questions.explanation:
Wernicke encephalopathy is an acute condition characterised by classic triad of confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus. However, the triad only seen in 10% of cases ; confusion in 80% of cases. It occurs secondary to thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 606.

questions.question_text: All of the following domains of cognition are crucial for successful completion of this task except
questions.explanation:
The clock-drawing test does not assess one’s orientation to time.
Ref: https://www.sralab.org/sites/default/files/2017-07/Clock%20Drawing%20Test%20Instructions.pdf

questions.question_text: These symptoms suggest that a tumour, if present, is most likely to be located in the
questions.explanation:
Lesions of the frontal lobes are characterised by changes in personality. The frontal lobe syndrome, which is most commonly produced by trauma, infarcts, tumours, multiple sclerosis, or frontotemporal dementia, consists of slow thinking, poor judgement, decreased curiosity, social withdrawal, and irritability. Patients may display apathetic indifference to experience that suddenly explode into impulsive disinhibition.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 935.

questions.question_text: Alexia without agraphia (pure alexia) is seen in lesions of
questions.explanation: In alexia without agraphia or pure word blindness, patients retain the ability to write, but are unable to read (even words that they have just written) and often have right homonymous hemianopia. This disorder results from the loss of visual input to the language area [usually the dominant (left) angular gyrus] without the involvement of the language area or output from the language area to the motor cortex. The ability to process visual input into language (i.e. reading) is lost in these patients. The pathways involved in this syndrome are believed to be localized to the inferior portion of the splenium of the corpus callosum on the side of the dominant (usually left) cerebral hemisphere. This is associated with posterior cerebral artery damage.

questions.question_text: What type of statement is this?
questions.explanation: Affirmative statements that are genuine and appropriate indicating respect and dignity offer positive reinforcement during a psychiatric interview.

questions.question_text: All of the following help localizing a neurological lesion to cerebellum EXCEPT
questions.explanation: Cerebellar signs: Ataxia, hypotonia, dyssynergia (incoordination), dysmetria (past pointing), dysdiadochokinesis, dysrhythmia and dysarthria

questions.question_text: Various components of language that must be tested in order to localize the brain lesion causing aphasia include all EXCEPT
questions.explanation: Reading, writing, repetition, fluency, comprehension and naming are tested to localize aphasia..

questions.question_text: In occasional cannabis user, how long is cannabis detected in urine after last use?
questions.explanation:
In the setting of occasional use, cannabis can be detected in the urine for up to 3 days.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 631.

questions.question_text: Which artery is most likely to be implicated in this presentation?
questions.explanation:
Damage to the anterior cingulate cortex is known to be a primary cause for akinesia and mutism and has frequently been described in case reports of patients with bleeding, stroke, or other types of severe brain injury. The most dramatic examples of akinesia and mutism follow bilateral lesions of the anterior cingulate cortex, such as after bilateral damage to the vascular supply of the anterior cerebral artery territory.
Ref: Arnts H, van Erp WS, Lavrijsen JC, van Gaal S, Groenewegen HJ, van den Munckhof P. On the pathophysiology and treatment of akinetic mutism. Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews. 2020 May 1;112:270-8.

questions.question_text: Inability to attend to the parts and the whole of an object at the same time is called
questions.explanation:
Simultanagnosia refers to impairment in the perception or integration of visual stimuli appearing simultaneously.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1144.

questions.question_text: Select the most appropriate investigation for a patient on antipsychotic medications presenting with weight gain, excessive thirst and fatigue.
questions.explanation: The symptoms of weight gain, excessive thirst and fatigue are suggestive of impaired glucose tolerance. A fasting blood glucose is indicated to diagnose antipsychotic related diabetes mellitus.

questions.question_text: Which of the following signs is highly likely in this case?

options.text: Xanthomas on extensor aspect of forearm

questions.explanation:
Wilson disease is a genetic disorder of copper metabolism that leads to copper accumulation in various organs, primarily the liver and brain. Clinical symptoms are a result of organ dysfunction due to the direct or indirect effects of copper accumulation. It is typically described as a hepato-neurological disease, with focus on signs of liver disease and extrapyramidal symptoms (e.g. tremor, dystonia, dysarthria). Psychiatric symptoms include personality disturbances (e.g. antisocial behaviour, irritability, disinhibition), mood abnormalities (e.g. bipolar, depression, suicide attempts), psychosis, and cognitive impairment. Kayser-Fleischer rings (green-brown copper deposits on Descemet’s membrane of the cornea) are present in 95% of patients with neurological symptoms, in 50-60% of patients without neurological symptoms, and in only 10% of asymptomatic siblings.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 166.
Litwin T et al. Psychiatric manifestations in Wilson’s disease: possibilities and difficulties for treatment. Therapeutic advances in psychopharmacology. 2018 Jul;8(7):199-211.

questions.question_text: The most appropriate description for executive function is

options.text: The capacity to identify stimulus that induces a perception
The capacity of controlling emotion and impulse
The capacity of purposefully applying one's physical skill
The capacity of accomplishing goal-directed behaviour

correct_answer.text: The capacity of accomplishing goal-directed behaviour

correct_answers.text: The capacity of accomplishing goal-directed behaviour

questions.explanation:
As conceptualised by Muriel Lezak, the executive functions include volition (i.e. formulation of a goal, motivation to achieve the goal, and awareness of one’s own ability to achieve the goal), planning, purposive action (response selection and initiation, maintenance, switching, and stopping), and execution (which involves self-monitoring and self-correction as well as control of the spatiotemporal aspects of the response).
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 50.

questions.question_text: What is the most likely psychiatric cause?
questions.explanation:
In factitious disorder, patients intentionally falsify their symptoms and past history and fabricate signs of physical or mental disorder, with the primary aim of obtaining medical attention and treatment. This patient's repeated presentation to a surgical ward (probably with various pain symptoms leading to surgeries) is suggestive of a factitious disorder.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 876.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about narcoanalysis is NOT true?

options.text: Useful technique when repression and dissociation are suspected.
Organic muteness gets better with amobarbital infusion
Psychogenic muteness gets better with amobarbital infusion

correct_answer.text: Organic muteness gets better with amobarbital infusion

correct_answers.text: Organic muteness gets better with amobarbital infusion

questions.explanation: Interviews with amobarbital have both diagnostic and therapeutic indications. These are sometimes helpful in differentiating nonorganic and organic conditions, particularly in patients with symptoms of catatonia, stupor, and muteness. Organic conditions tend to worsen with infusions of amobarbital, but nonorganic or psychogenic conditions tend to get better because of disinhibition, decreased anxiety, or increased relaxation. Therapeutically, amobarbital interviews are useful in disorders of repression and dissociation such as amnesia and fugue. Benzodiazepines can be substituted for amobarbital.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is characteristic of a senile pupil?

options.text: Sluggish accommodation reaction; preserved light reaction
Preserved accommodation reaction; sluggish light reaction
No changes in light and accommodation reaction

questions.explanation: The pupil size becomes smaller with aging. This constricting of pupil is called senile miosis; the pupil becomes sluggish to light and accommodation.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a test of parietal lobe functioning?
questions.explanation: Tests of parietal lobe functioning include finger agnosia, astereognosia, dysgraphaesthesia, two-point discrimination, and right-left orientation. Although of disputed clinical value, Gerstmann syndrome is classically described as right-left disorientation, finger agnosia, dysgraphia, and dyscalculia, due to a lesion of the dominant (usually left) parietal lobe.

questions.question_text: Which of the following cognitive domains is assessed by Wisconsin Card Sorting Test?
questions.explanation:
The Wisconsin card sorting task is a test of frontal lobe functioning. The patient has to determine the rule for card allocation and allocate cards accordingly. When the rule changes, a patient with frontal lobe dysfunction is likely to make more errors (tests response inhibition and set shifting).
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 60.

questions.question_text: He is most likely to have
questions.explanation:
Distinctive qualitative errors in constructing block designs and in drawing a complex geometric configuration (e.g., Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure test) can be seen with either right or left hemisphere damage. In the presence of lateralised damage to the right hemisphere, impaired performance often reflects the patient’s inability to appreciate the “Gestalt” or global features of a design. In contrast, damage to the left hemisphere commonly results in inaccurate reproduction of internal details of the design, but the Gestalt is more likely to be preserved.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 48-49.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a risk factor for QT prolongation on ECG?
questions.explanation:
Risk factors for QTc prolongation include hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypocalcaemia, arrythmias, bradycardia, extremes of age, and female gender.
Ref: Taylor DM, Gaughran F, Pillinger T. The Maudsley Practice Guidelines for Physical Health Conditions in Psychiatry. 2021. pp. 26-27.

questions.question_text: In MMSE, intersecting pentagons test primarily assesses which of the following functions?
questions.explanation:
Praxis refers to a complex cognitive function, in which the motor system is used to execute complex learned actions and movements, such as the copying of drawings. Constructional praxis declines with age and can become impaired by several neurodegenerative diseases. Usual tasks to evaluate this function include the copying of drawings or drawing three-dimensional shapes. In the MMSE, praxis is evaluated by drawing two intersecting pentagons, in which the interconnected area should be shaped like a rhombus. Praxis functions depend mainly on the parietal lobe, which is specialised for visuospatial information, visual attention, body position, and whole body object perception relative to self.
Ref: Martinelli JE et al. Performance of the Pentagon Drawing test for the screening of older adults with Alzheimer's dementia. Dementia & neuropsychologia. 2018 Mar;12(1):54-60.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a good technique to use for a poor historian?

options.text: Collecting information in parts over multiple interviews
Shifting to the neutral ground when necessary

questions.explanation: Use of open-ended questions and commands to increase the flow of information, use of continuation techniques to keep the flow coming and shifting to the neutral ground when necessary are useful techniques for a poor historian.

questions.question_text: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The biological basis of panic disorder has been postulated to be aberrant metabolic activity induced by lactate, from studies involving exercise-induced panic attacks and replicated by IV lactate infusion.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 370.

questions.question_text: The presence of intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies is a microscopic finding in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Pathologically, dementia with Lewy bodies is characterised by the presence of Lewy bodies – intraneuronal inclusions consisting mainly of alpha-synuclein aggregates and ubiquitin – in the neocortex, forebrain, brainstem, and other parts of the nervous system.
Ref: Mueller C et al. The prognosis of dementia with Lewy bodies. The Lancet Neurology. 2017 May 1;16(5):390-8.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a compound question?

options.text: I think you are not well. Am I right?
What can I do for you?
What is the average height of British women?
Do you know how IQ is calculated?
Do you go on holidays and are you able to relax then?

correct_answer.text: Do you go on holidays and are you able to relax then?

correct_answers.text: Do you go on holidays and are you able to relax then?

questions.explanation: Adding two or more questions in a single statement is referred to as a compound question. This confuses the patient and may lead to either a vague response or no response.

questions.question_text: Which of the following tasks is most useful in evaluating a patient's ability to concentrate?

options.text: Estimating the distance between Sheffield and London

questions.explanation: Serial Sevens is a clinical test that forms a part of the Mini Mental Status Examination; it is a quick and easy test of concentration and memory, used especially if there is a clinical suspicion of cognitive dysfunction.

questions.question_text: One of the most well established anatomical changes seen in schizophrenia is
questions.explanation:
Brain structural abnormalities are widely reported in schizophrenia with large-scale meta-analyses detecting a smaller hippocampal volume in patients compared to controls, followed by a smaller amygdala, thalamus, nucleus accumbens, and intracranial volumes, as well as larger pallidum and larger lateral ventricle volumes.
Ref: Keshavan MS, Collin G, Guimond S, Kelly S, Prasad KM, Lizano P. Neuroimaging in schizophrenia. Neuroimaging Clinics. 2020 Feb 1;30(1):73-83.

questions.question_text: The symptom or sign that responds earlier than others when thiamine is replaced in a patient with Wernicke's encephalopathy is
questions.explanation: Ophthalmoplegia responds within hours, but cognitive impairment takes longer.

questions.question_text: Which of the following arteries on occlusion leads to symptoms suggestive of dorsolateral prefrontal dysfunction?
questions.explanation: DLPFC consists of the lateral portions of Brodmann areas 9 - 12, areas 45, 46, and the superior part of area 47. These regions receive their blood supply from the middle cerebral artery.

questions.question_text: Copying intersecting polygons in MMSE tests the functions of
questions.explanation:
Praxis refers to a complex cognitive function, in which the motor system is used to execute complex learned actions and movements, such as the copying of drawings. Constructional praxis declines with age and can become impaired by several neurodegenerative diseases. Usual tasks to evaluate this function include the copying of drawings or drawing three-dimensional shapes. In the MMSE, praxis is evaluated by drawing two intersecting pentagons, in which the interconnected area should be shaped like a rhombus. Praxis functions depend mainly on the parietal lobe, which is specialised for visuospatial information, visual attention, body position, and whole body object perception relative to self.
Ref: Martinelli JE et al. Performance of the Pentagon Drawing test for the screening of older adults with Alzheimer's dementia. Dementia & neuropsychologia. 2018 Mar;12(1):54-60.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is true concerning bedside tests of orientation?

options.text: Most patients do not remember the length of time spent in hospital in spite of intact orientation
Orientation to time is often affected in delirium
Disorientation to one's own name indicates hippocampal lesions
Orientation to person is the most sensitive test

correct_answer.text: Orientation to time is often affected in delirium

correct_answers.text: Orientation to time is often affected in delirium

questions.explanation:
Orientation is usually assessed to time, place and person; it is not particularly sensitive, and intact orientation does not exclude a significant memory disorder, particularly if there is concern about memory from an informant. Time orientation is the most helpful, and should include the time of day. Many normal people do not know the exact date, and being out by two days or less is considered normal when scoring this formally. Time intervals are often poorly monitored by patients with delirium, moderate to severe dementia, and in the amnesic syndrome, and are easily tested by asking about the length of time spent in hospital. Person orientation includes name, age, and date of birth. Disorientation to one's own name is usually only seen in psychogenic amnesia.
Ref: Cognitive assessment for clinicians -- Kipps and Hodges 76 .., http://jnnp.bmj.com/content/76/suppl_1/i22.full (accessed May 6, 2021)

questions.question_text: The reason for using confrontation technique during a clinical interview is to

options.text: Reveal some absurd notions that patients might hold
Make patients stop lying to the clinician
Help the patient face a difficult aspect of their problems
Clarify certain associations that patients may not see

correct_answer.text: Help the patient face a difficult aspect of their problems

correct_answers.text: Help the patient face a difficult aspect of their problems

questions.explanation: Confrontation technique points out to a patient something to which the doctor thinks the patient is missing or denying. This must be done in a respectful way with an aim to help patients face a difficult aspect rather than dismissing patients by pointing out a negative aspect.

questions.question_text: Amphetamines could be detected in urine for up to
questions.explanation:
Amphetamines can be detected in the urine for up to 48 hours.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 631.

questions.question_text: What is her body mass index?
questions.explanation:
Body mass index (BMI) is a ratio between weight and height and is more useful for predicting health risks than weight alone. BMI = Weight (in kg)/height (in m)².
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 410.

questions.question_text: Unilateral frontal lobe damage can result in
questions.explanation: Damage to upper motor neurons originating in frontal motor strip can result in contralateral spastic hemiparesis.

questions.question_text: Which of the following conditions, when suspected, will necessitate performing a neurological procedure called Hoover's test?
questions.explanation: Hoover's test is useful to identify patients with conversion disorder, who has paralysis with One or more limbs or one side of the face or body may be affected. Here the patient is unable to raise the affected limb from the couch but can raise the unaffected limb against resistance with demonstrable pressing down of the heel on the affected side. Ref: Oxford handbook of psychiatry; 746

questions.question_text: Patients with schizophrenia are least likely to perform poorly on which of the following tests?

options.text: Trail B of the Halstead-Reitan battery

questions.explanation: Patients with schizophrenia perform far more poorly than controls on category test (assess higher-order reasoning), Wisconsin card sort test (tests higher-order reasoning), speech sounds perception test, Trail B of the Halstead-Reitan battery (tests the ability to shift flexibility between cognitive sets). Tests of overall cognitive ability such as MMSE are usually intact in schizophrenia.

questions.question_text: Which of the following signs can be elicited by having the patient extend both arms with the wrists dorsiflexed and palms facing forward and eyes closed?
questions.explanation:
Asterixis can be elicited by having the patient extend both arms with the wrists dorsiflexed and palms facing forward and eyes closed. Brief jerky downward movements of the wrist are considered a positive sign. Asterixis is commonly seen with metabolic encephalopathies.
Ref: Neurological History and Physical Examination - Medscape, http://emedicine.medscape.com/article/1147993-overview (accessed May 5, 2021)

questions.question_text: The wavelet of EEG that is greater than 13 Hz in frequency is
questions.explanation:
Alpha waves: frequency range 8-13 Hz; highly rhythmic and constitute the dominant brain wave frequency of the normal eyes-closed awake EEG
Beta waves: frequencies that are faster than the upper 13 Hz limit of the alpha rhythm; not uncommon in average adult waking EEG studies, particularly over the frontal-central regions
Delta waves: frequency of 3.5 Hz or less; not present in the normal waking EEG, but a prominent feature of deeper stages of sleep; presence of significant generalised or focal delta waves in the awake EEG is strongly indicative of a pathophysiological process
Theta waves: frequency 4-7.5 Hz; small amount of sporadic, arrhythmic, and isolated theta activity can be seen in many normal waking EEG studies, particularly in frontal-temporal regions; a prominent feature of the drowsy and sleep tracing; excessive theta in awake EEG, generalised, or focal, suggests the operation of a pathologic process
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 998-999.

questions.question_text: Failure of object recognition despite normal sensory input and motor functions is called
questions.explanation:
Anosognosia: inability to recognise a physical deficit in oneself (e.g. patient denies paralysed limb)
Visual agnosia: inability to recognise objects
Prosopagnosia: inability to recognise familiar faces that is not due to impaired visual acuity or level of consciousness
Astereognosis: inability to recognise familiar objects by touch
Neglect: failure to detect visual or tactile stimuli or to move the limb in the contralateral hemispace
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 49, 1136, 1143, 1145.

questions.question_text: In schizophrenia, the anatomical structure in the brain that is most consistently reduced in size is
questions.explanation: Most of the listed structures have been observed to have structural abnormalities in schizophrenia. In fact, the hippocampus has been repeatedly shown to have a reduced volume though not in all studies. Insula, which forms a part of the paralimbic cotex, has been unequivocally shown to have volumetric abnormalities in schizophrenia. Other consistently affected structures include anterior cingulate cortex, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and thalamus.

questions.question_text: Which of the following laboratory tests should be conducted prior to initiating lithium treatment?
questions.explanation:
Prior to commencing lithium therapy, conduct the following:
- Physical examination
- Full blood count
- Urea and electrolytes
- Thyroid function tests
- Renal function
- Baseline weight and height (body mass index)
- If clinically indicated: ECG, pregnancy test
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 350.

questions.question_text: In MRS, which nuclei are commonly used for in vivo measure of phosphocreatinine?
questions.explanation:
Whereas routine MRI detects hydrogen nuclei to determine brain structure, magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) can detect several odd-numbered nuclei. The readout of an MRS device is usually in the form of a spectrum, such as those for phosphorous-31 and hydrogen-1 nuclei. The MRS of the hydrogen-1 nuclei is best at measuring N-acetylaspartate (NAA), creatine, and choline-containing molecules, but can also detect glutamate, glutamine, lactate, and myo-inositol. MRS of phosphorous-31 can be used to determine the concentrations of phosphorous-containing compounds (e.g. ATP, GTP, phosphocreatinine).
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 71-72.

questions.question_text: A patient has normal accommodation reflex but no reaction on testing light reflex. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
An Argyll-Robertson pupil is a pupil of the eye that manifests accommodation by constricting when watching a finger that is brought close to the face but does not respond to light by constricting, a neurological sign of damage to the midbrain relays of the oculomotor nerve. In 1869, Douglas Argyll-Robertson described several patients whose pupils reacted poorly to light with a normal near response. Later the aetiology of this pupillary anomaly was discovered to be tertiary syphilis. Currently, diabetes leads the list of causes for the so called Argyll-Robertson Pupil or ARP.
Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Which of the following laboratory test is indicated?
questions.explanation: The scenario depicts acute intermittent porphyria (AIP). It is one of the groups of disorders of haem metabolism, characterised by neurological and psychiatric manifestations without obvious cutaneous markers. AIP manifests itself by abdomen pain, neuropathies, and constipation, but, unlike most types of porphyria, patients with AIP do not have a rash. It is an autosomal dominant disorder with the presentation starting between ages 18 and 40. It is episodic in nature and the episodes are often triggered by certain medications including estrogens, barbiturates and benzodiazepines. Diclofenac can precipitate an episode. Psychiatric manifestations include depression, anxiety, delirium and psychosis. Most important lab test is demonstrating increased urinary porphobilinogen during acute attacks. Treatment is aimed at reducing haem synthesis by administering haemin

questions.question_text: Which one of the following has been used in vitro as a powerful method of analytical chemistry and enables the measurement of the concentration of different metabolites in the brain?
questions.explanation:
Magnetic resonance spectroscopy enables information to be obtained about the biochemistry of tissues, which can be compared to identify tissue change following strokes or tumours. It enables detection of differences that may precede structural changes detectable with MRI.
Ref: Martinelli C, Shergill SS. Everything you wanted to know about neuroimaging and psychiatry, but were afraid to ask. BJPsych Advances. 2015 Jul;21(4):251-60.

questions.question_text: Select the best imaging technique to diagnose her condition.
questions.explanation:
Reduced dopamine transporter (DAT) uptake in basal ganglia demonstrated by SPECT or PET imaging is an indicative biomarker of dementia with Lewy bodies. The utility of DAT imaging in distinguishing dementia with Lewy bodies from Alzheimer dementia is well-established, with sensitivity (78%) and specificity (90%).
Ref: McKeith IG et al. Diagnosis and management of dementia with Lewy bodies: Fourth consensus report of the DLB Consortium. Neurology. 2017 Jul 4;89(1):88-100.

questions.question_text: A non-invasive perfusion MRI methodology used to quantify cerebral blood flow is
questions.explanation:
Arterial spin labelling is a magnetic resonance imaging perfusion technique that enables quantification of cerebral blood flow without the use of gadolinium contrast.
Ref: Ho ML. Arterial spin labeling: clinical applications. Journal of Neuroradiology. 2018 Sep 1;45(5):276-89.

questions.question_text: Which of the following questions is useful in evaluating immediate recall?

options.text: Can you tell me today's date?
What did you have for dinner?
Where did you go to school?
Can you repeat these six numbers?

correct_answer.text: Can you repeat these six numbers?

correct_answers.text: Can you repeat these six numbers?

questions.explanation:
Immediate memory refers to the amount of information that can be held in mind (like a phone number or digit span) to be available for immediate use.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 13.

questions.question_text: Letter cancellation, star cancellation and line bisection tasks examine which of the following cognitive dysfunction?
questions.explanation:
Visual neglect can be assessed with cancellation and line bisection tasks, in which the paper is placed at the patient’s midline, and the patient is asked to either cross out stars/letters/lines on the page or bisect the single line presented.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 49.

questions.question_text: REM pattern is recorded during the daytime in a student who has been studying for exams the last two weeks. The most likely reason is
questions.explanation: REM sleep during daytime can be seen in narcolepsy, sleep deprivation or withdrawal from stimulants.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a component of clock drawing test?

options.text: Using numbers 1 to 12 to create the face of a clock
Being aware of the current time when the test is administered
Indicating the hour correctly according to instructions
Indicating the minutes correctly according to instructions
Placing the hands of the clock correctly

correct_answer.text: Being aware of the current time when the test is administered

correct_answers.text: Being aware of the current time when the test is administered

questions.explanation:
The clock-drawing test does not assess one’s orientation to time.
Ref: https://www.sralab.org/sites/default/files/2017-07/Clock%20Drawing%20Test%20Instructions.pdf

questions.question_text: Which of the following has a white, bright appearance in a CT scan?
questions.explanation: The CT image is determined by the degree to which tissues absorb X-irradiation. The bony structures absorb high amounts of irradiation and tend to obscure details of neighbouring structures, an especially troubling problem in the brainstem, which is surrounded by a thick skull base. In a CT scan, CSF appears black, brain tissue appears grey, and the skull appears white. There is very poor discrimination between grey and white matter of the brain. Blood appears bright white. Certain tumours may be invisible on CT because they absorb as much irradiation as the surrounding normal brain. In comparison with MRI, the only component of the brain better seen on CT scanning is calcification, which may be invisible on MRI. T1 MRI images are the most similar to CT images. Blood appears bright in both CT and T1 MRI.

questions.question_text: The transition of patients from ultra high risk to psychotic patients involves a volume reduction in which part of the brain region?
questions.explanation:
Ultra high-risk patients that transition to psychosis have been reported to exhibit greater longitudinal volume reduction and/or cortical thinning in frontal areas (including orbitofrontal, superior frontal, middle frontal, and prefrontal cortices); temporal areas (such as the inferior and middle temporal cortex, and the fusiform and parahippocampal cortex); the medical and superior parietal lobes and precuneus; and the insular cortex.
Ref: Andreou C, Borgwardt S. Structural and functional imaging markers for susceptibility to psychosis. Molecular psychiatry. 2020 Nov;25(11):2773-85.

questions.question_text: Generalised diffuse delta and theta waves in the EEG are seen in
questions.explanation:
Diffuse slowing of the background rhythms of the EEG is the most common abnormality. It is non-specific and is present in patients with diffuse encephalopathies of diverse causes. The slowing of background activity in a metabolic encephalopathy usually begins with an increase in theta activity, followed by intermittent generalised theta slowing or bilateral synchronous delta waves groups, sometimes with a frontal maximum (frontal intermittent rhythmic delta activity).
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 999.
Boutros NN, Galderisi S, Pogarell O, Riggio S. Standard electroencephalography in clinical psychiatry: A practical handbook. 2011. p. 72.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is an advantage of CT scans over MRI?

options.text: Gray vs. white matter demarcation is well delineated
Posterior fossa lesions are well noted
Lesions close to bone are better seen

questions.explanation:
The CT image is determined by the degree to which tissues absorb X-irradiation. The bony structures absorb high amounts of irradiation and tend to obscure details of neighbouring structures, an especially troubling problem in the brainstem, which is surrounded by a thick skull base. In a CT scan, CSF appears black, brain tissue appears grey, and the skull appears white. There is very poor discrimination between grey and white matter of the brain. Blood appears bright white. Certain tumours may be invisible on CT because they absorb as much irradiation as the surrounding normal brain. In comparison with MRI, the only component of the brain better seen on CT scanning is calcification, which may be invisible on MRI.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 69-70.

questions.question_text: Choose the most likely cause for his presentation.
questions.explanation:
Psychogenic polydipsia is characterised by excessive fluid intake without an organic cause. A low plasma sodium concentration with a low urine osmolality is usually indicative of water overload due to psychogenic polydipsia. A high-normal plasma concentration in conjunction with a urine osmolality that is lower than plasma osmolality points towards diabetes insipidus.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 116.
Taylor DM, Gaughran F, Pillinger T. The Maudsley Practice Guidelines for Physical Health Conditions in Psychiatry. 2021. p. 269.

questions.question_text: What technique is he using?
questions.explanation:
Summation can be used periodically during the interview in order to summarise what has been identified about a certain topic. This provides the opportunity for the patient to clarify or modify the psychiatrist’s understanding and possibly add new material.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 14.

questions.question_text: The most likely diagnosis is
questions.explanation:
“Heroin-associated nephropathy” is the term used to describe focal segmental glomerulosclerosis in the setting of heroin use. Patients present with proteinuria, which may be in the nephrotic range. It is more common among Black heroin users.
Ref: Sethi, S. The changing spectrum of heroin-associated kidney disease. CJASN. 2018: 975-976.

questions.question_text: Inappropriate lack of concern about a functional deficit or disability is known as
questions.explanation:
(La) belle indifference is a surprising lack of concern for, or denial of, apparently severe functional disability. It is part of classical descriptions of hysteria and continues to be associated with operational descriptions of conversion disorder. It is also seen in medical illnesses (e.g. following a stroke) and is a rare and non-specific symptom of no diagnostic value.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 103.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a functional neuroimaging technique?
questions.explanation: Functional neuroimaging measures an aspect of brain function to understand the relationship between activity in certain brain areas and specific mental functions. Common methods of functional neuroimaging include SPECT, PET, fMRI, EEG and NIRS (near infra-red spectroscopic imaging). Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA) is a powerful technique for the visualization of blood vessels in the human body. DSA is a fluoroscopy technique to visualize blood vessels in a bony or dense, soft tissue area. It does not measure brain function as such but identifies abnormalities in the integrity of cerebral vasculature.

questions.question_text: Which of the following lesions is most likely to be present?

options.text: Thoracic spinal cord lesion at T12

questions.explanation: A pronator drift is elicited by having the patient extend both arms with the wrists supinated and palms facing upwards and eyes closed - slow unequal drift towards pronation indicates hemiparetic weakness. The left arm drop in this case indicates a right cerebral lesion.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a frontal release sign?
questions.explanation:
Primitive reflexes include the glabellar tap, rooting, snout, sucking, and palmomental reflexes. These are generally absent in adults. When present in the adult, these signs signify diffuse cerebral damage, particularly of the frontal lobes (hence called frontal-lobe release signs). Cremasteric reflex is a superficial reflex.
Ref: Neurological History and Physical Examination - Medscape, http://emedicine.medscape.com/article/1147993-overview (accessed May 6, 2021)

questions.question_text: Clinical features of drug-induced hyponatraemia include
questions.explanation:
Symptoms and signs of drug-induced hyponatraemia can range from nausea, muscle cramps/weakness, and malaise to hypertension, lethargy, confusion, and, if severe, seizures and coma.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 1026.

questions.question_text: Blood oxygen level dependent measurement BOLD is a technique used in which of the following imaging modalities?
questions.explanation:
The goal of fMRI is to visualise brain activity and so spatial resolution is sacrificed to the benefit of temporal resolution. fMRI is not at sufficient temporal resolution to directly measure the neuronal signal and so it measures an indirect index of neuronal activity – the blood oxygen-level dependent (BOLD) contrast. The principle behind BOLD is that an active population of neurons will receive more fresh, oxygen-risk blood flow than non-active neurons. It is this variation between the magnetic signal of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood in the brain that constitutes the basis for the fMRI signal.
Ref: Martinelli C, Shergill SS. Everything you wanted to know about neuroimaging and psychiatry, but were afraid to ask. BJPsych Advances. 2015 Jul;21(4):251-60.

questions.question_text: A patient can follow commands and repeat phrases, but he has incomprehensible speech. He is likely to have
questions.explanation:
When repetition is preserved in a patient with Broca (non-fluent) aphasia, it signifies transcortical motor aphasia, and the lesion is anterior to the Broca area. When repetition is preserved in Wernicke (fluent) aphasia, it is called transcortical sensory aphasia, and the lesion is posterior to the Wernicke area.
Ref: Neurological History and Physical Examination - Medscape, http://emedicine.medscape.com/article/1147993-overview (accessed May 6, 2021)

questions.question_text: The earliest appearance of brain atrophy in Alzheimer disease is most marked in which of the following brain regions?
questions.explanation:
Alzheimer disease is associated with medial temporal lobe atrophy, particularly of the entorhinal cortex and hippocampus.
Ref: McKhann, G.M. et al. 2011. The diagnosis of dementia due to Alzheimer's disease: recommendations from the National Institute on Aging‐Alzheimer's Association workgroups on diagnostic guidelines for Alzheimer's disease. Alzheimer's & dementia, 7(3), pp.263-269.

questions.question_text: This patient is most likely to have a lesion in which of the following structures?
questions.explanation: Thalamo-parietal projections, when damaged, can give rise to the above reported sensory disturbances in addition to disturbances in higher sensory integration resulting in failed 2 point discrimination and stereognosis.

questions.question_text: How long will it be present in his urine?
questions.explanation:
Cannabis can be detected in urine after single use for up to 3 days. In the setting of chronic, heavy use, cannabis can be detected in the urine for up to 4 weeks.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 631.

questions.question_text: Inability to recognise familiar faces is seen in
questions.explanation:
Prosopagnosia is the inability to recognise familiar faces that is not due to impaired visual acuity or level of consciousness.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1143.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a supportive technique not aimed at eliciting information?
questions.explanation: Validation helps to decrease a patient's sense of embarrassment about a feeling or behaviour. Validation is often employed when quoting how it is normal for people to have different emotions/ reactions/ behaviours, etc.

questions.question_text: Which of the following will you use to assess orientation in a hospitalised patient?

options.text: Ability to repeat a phone number immediately after reading out
Tap the table once whenever the examiner reads letter 'E' from a random list of alphabets
Ability to recognise pictures of famous personalities
Ability to correctly identify the doctor when asked to point out
Ability to remember his/her own address

correct_answer.text: Ability to correctly identify the doctor when asked to point out

correct_answers.text: Ability to correctly identify the doctor when asked to point out

questions.explanation: Orientation to person is a stable domain which is generally lost only late in the course of a confusional state.

questions.question_text: Which of the following investigations involve introducing a synthetic radionucleotide for obtaining brain images?
questions.explanation:
Both PET and SPECT are based on the idea that it is possible to learn about a dynamic process by introducing a measurable tracer into a target system and then tracking it as it travels around the system. Both PET and SPECT involve the administration of a radiopharmaceutical tracer which, once absorbed, emits gamma rays that can be detected by the scanner and thus provide an image of the distribution of the tracer in the body over time.
Ref: Martinelli C, Shergill SS. Everything you wanted to know about neuroimaging and psychiatry, but were afraid to ask. BJPsych Advances. 2015 Jul;21(4):251-60.

questions.question_text: All of the following drugs will increase urine porphyrins in a susceptible individual with disordered haem metabolism except
questions.explanation: Acute intermittent porphyria is episodic in nature and the episodes are often triggered by certain medications including estrogens, barbiturates and benzodiazepines. Diclofenac can precipitate an episode. Psychiatric manifestations include depression, anxiety, delirium and psychosis.

questions.question_text: The investigation that has no helpful role in diagnosing narcolepsy is
questions.explanation:
The sleep deprivation test is not helpful to diagnose narcolepsy.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 451.

questions.question_text: Which of the following speech best describes Broca aphasia?
questions.explanation:
Broca aphasia (also called non-fluent or expressive aphasia) had traditionally been characterised by non-fluent speech and impaired repetition but intact auditory comprehension.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 48.

questions.question_text: All of the following are signs of an upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion except
questions.explanation:
An upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion is a lesion anywhere from the cortex to the corticospinal tract. There are both positive and negative features of the UMN syndrome. Positive features include hyperreflexia, spasticity, and a positive Babinski reflex (presenting as an upward response of the big toe when the plantar surface of the foot is stored, with other toes fanning out). Negative features include impaired motor control, easy fatiguability, weakness, and loss of dexterity. Lower motor neuron (LMN) syndromes may arise from pathology affecting the distal motor nerve up to the level of the anterior horn cell. LMN lesions are characterised by muscle atrophy, weakness (like UMN lesions), and hyporeflexia without sensory involvement. Atrophy is seen in LMN lesions, not in UMN lesions.
Ref: Garg N et al. Differentiating lower motor neuron syndromes. Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery & Psychiatry. 2017 Jun 1;88(6):474-83.

questions.question_text: Which region of the brain is often highlighted when performing tasks inside a scanner during a functional MRI scan?
questions.explanation: The region of the brain that is often highlighted by functional MRI scan is the primary motor cortex.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Generalised lymph node enlargement with muscle wasting along with social withdrawal (possibly due to perceived stigma) is suggestive of a HIV illness.

questions.question_text: T1 images in MRI are mostly useful for
questions.explanation:
The T1 image most closely resembles that of CT scans and is most useful for assessing overall brain structure. T1 is also the only sequence that allows contrast enhancement with the contrast agent gadolinium-diethylenetriamine pentaacetic acid.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 70.

questions.question_text: How many points has he lost in total?
questions.explanation: 5 points are awarded for orientation in time and 3 points for recall.

questions.question_text: Anomic dysphasia is suggestive of a lesion in which of the following regions of the brain?
questions.explanation: In anomic dysphasia, confrontation naming is affected more than any other function (when an object is shown, the patient cannot tell its name). It is often due to small left-sided lesions in language cortex - temporo-parietal junction.

questions.question_text: Confrontation test carried out during physical examination is useful to detect which one of the following?
questions.explanation:
Confrontation test is used to assess visual fields with a wiggling finger or a red pin.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 128.

questions.question_text: A tremor that decreases with volitional movements and appears primarily when not engaged in tasks is most likely to be a
questions.explanation:
A resting tremor occurs in a body part that is relaxed and completely supported against gravity (e.g., when resting on the arm of a chair). It is typically enhanced by mental stress (e.g., counting backward) or movement of another body part (e.g., walking) and diminished by voluntary movement. Resting tremor is most commonly caused by parkinsonism, but may also occur in severe essential tremor.
Ref: Crawford III PF, Zimmerman EE. Tremor: sorting through the differential diagnosis. American family physician. 2018 Feb 1;97(3):180-6.

questions.question_text: An important investigation useful to differentiate Lewy body dementia from Alzheimer disease is
questions.explanation:
Reduced dopamine transporter (DAT) uptake in basal ganglia demonstrated by SPECT or PET imaging is an indicative biomarker of dementia with Lewy bodies. The utility of DAT imaging in distinguishing dementia with Lewy bodies from Alzheimer dementia is well-established, with sensitivity (78%) and specificity (90%).
Ref: McKeith IG et al. Diagnosis and management of dementia with Lewy bodies: Fourth consensus report of the DLB Consortium. Neurology. 2017 Jul 4;89(1):88-100.

questions.question_text: Which of the following cognitive dysfunctions is he describing?
questions.explanation:
Anterograde amnesia is the period of amnesia between an event (e.g. head injury) and the resumption of continuous memory. The length of anterograde amnesia is correlated with the extent of the brain injury.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 102.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following techniques can measure the extent of myelination of white matter fibres at a macroscopic level?
questions.explanation:
Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) allows imaging of the organisation and orientation of brain white matter fibres by using the information derived from the movement of water molecules inside the tissues. DTI is an invaluable tool as it is at present the only method by which we can visualise white matter anatomy, which is still largely unknown.
Ref: Martinelli C, Shergill SS. Everything you wanted to know about neuroimaging and psychiatry, but were afraid to ask. BJPsych Advances. 2015 Jul;21(4):251-60.

questions.question_text: Which of the following levels of insight does he have?

options.text: Awareness of problems but denial of responsibility

questions.explanation: Intellectual insight: admission that the patient is ill and that symptoms or failures in social adjustment are caused by the patient's own particular irrational feelings or disturbances without applying this knowledge to future experiences.

questions.question_text: The brain region with most prominent changes observed using neuroimaging in ADHD is
questions.explanation:
Imaging studies have repeatedly shown underfunctioning of the frontostriatal pathways and underactivation of several prefrontal cortical areas, consistent with reduced cognitive executive functioning in ADHD.
Ref: Hill P. Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder in children and adolescents: Assessment and treatment. BJPsych Advances. 2015 Jan;21(1):23-30.

questions.question_text: With a secluded patient, behavioural observation is carried out every 5th minute through a glass window. This technique is called
questions.explanation: Behavioural observation methods include observing and recording behavioural events, to study mental state or plan intervention. They are of 2 types: Event sampling: e.g. every fifth or tenth event is coded in detail. Time sampling: observations may be made only every 5 or 10 mins.

questions.question_text: which of the following is least likely to be seen?
questions.explanation: Reduced short-term, working memory is a feature of dementia. It is not expected as a part of healthy aging. But reduced motor speed, visuospatial skills, attentional span, and decreased new learning ability are seen in healthy aging process.

questions.question_text: Which of the following endocrine changes is noted in anorexia nervosa?
questions.explanation: In adolescents and adults with anorexia nervosa, increased basal growth hormone (GH) secretion, a higher number of secretory bursts, and higher GH concentration is seen. This can have adverse effects on bone mass and eventual growth curve.

questions.question_text: Which of the following tests would be required to make a diagnosis of Huntington's disease in a patient without a family history?
questions.explanation:
The diagnosis of Huntington disease (HD) is straightforward if a patient with a known family history of HD presents with the typical neurological movement disorder (gene testing not required if there is laboratory confirmation of the Huntington disease gene in the family). In a patient without a family history, gene testing is essential but does not give a clinical diagnosis and must of combined with clinical history and physical exam.
Ref: Bachoud-Lévi AC et al. International Guidelines for the treatment of Huntington’s Disease. Frontiers in neurology. 2019;10:710.

questions.question_text: Which of the following clinical examination for apraxias is abnormal more commonly with a right than a left cerebral damage?
questions.explanation: Constructional apraxia is inability to construct elements to a meaningful whole (e.g. inability to draw or copy simple diagrams or figures). This is typically caused by a lesion in the right cerebral hemisphere.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a likely area of lesion?
questions.explanation: Categorization and error correction are tests for frontal lobe functioning.

questions.question_text: If this turns out to be a case of Balint syndrome, which of the following will NOT be a presenting feature?
questions.explanation:
Balint syndrome consists of a triad of simultanagnosia (inability to attend to more than one item of a complex scene at a time), optic ataxia (inability to guide reaching or pointing despite adequate vision), and oculomotor apraxia (inability to voluntarily direct saccades to a visual target). Fields may be full when challenged with gross stimuli, and oculocephalic reflexes are intact. This syndrome results from bilateral damage including the superior-parieto-occipital region, which disrupts the dorsal ('where') visual processing stream linking visual with parietal association areas. Possible causes include carbon monoxide poisoning, watershed infarction, leucodystrophy, and the posterior cortical variant of Alzheimer disease.
Ref: Cognitive assessment for clinicians -- Kipps and Hodges 76 .., http://jnnp.bmj.com/content/76/suppl_1/i22.full (accessed May 6, 2021)

questions.question_text: In which of the following conditions do you expect to see a pulvinar sign on magnetic resonance imaging?
questions.explanation:
The pulvinar sign on MRI is diagnostic of variant CJD. It refers to symmetric high-signal-intensity changes affecting the pulvinar and medial areas of the thalamus and the tectal plate seen on FLAIR sequence MRI.
Ref: Ortega-Cubero S et al. Structural and functional neuroimaging in human prion diseases. Neurología. 2013 Jun 1;28(5):299-308.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a test for executive function?
questions.explanation:
Visuospatial abilities (not executive function) can be assessed through procedures such as facial recognition and judgement of line orientation.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 54.

questions.question_text: Which neuroimaging modality can give information about metabolic changes in the brain?
questions.explanation:
As with fMRI, SPECT provides information on cerebral blood flow, which is highly correlated with the rate of glucose metabolism, but does not measure neuronal metabolism directly. A key difference between PET and SPECT is that PET can measure glucose metabolism and blood flow as indices of neuronal activity, whereas SPECT can only measure blood flow. Structural abnormalities, not metabolic changes, are detected by structural MRI and CT. Ultrasound imaging involves sending high-frequency sound waves to a target region and registering their returning echoes – images can be captured in real time and so movement of blood flow, organs, or fetus can be captured as well.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 73.
Martinelli C, Shergill SS. Everything you wanted to know about neuroimaging and psychiatry, but were afraid to ask. BJPsych Advances. 2015 Jul;21(4):251-60.

questions.question_text: In SPECT imaging iomazenil (I-123) is used to label
questions.explanation: Iomazenil is used for GABA-A receptors

questions.question_text: Which of the following interview technique is he using?
questions.explanation:
Reinforcement interventions are very important in patients sharing material about themselves and other influential individuals and events. Without these reinforcements, often, the interview will become less productive.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 14.

questions.question_text: This is called
questions.explanation: The Kernig's sign is elicited by flexing one hip and knee and then extending the knee with the hip still flexed. Hamstring spasm may occur; if severe, opposite knee may flex during the test - this is termed as a positive Kernig's.

questions.question_text: This type of memory is called
questions.explanation:
The performance of tasks such as typing, swimming, or cutting a loaf of bread are expressions of prior learning that differ from episodic memory in that there is no active awareness that memory is being searched in undertaking the particular skill. This type of memory is known as implicit, procedural, or skills memory. Studies of people with injury to the hippocampus suggest that declarative and implicit memory use different parts of the brain and can function independently. The hippocampus is believed to be the site where explicit (declarative) memory is stored, while implicit (procedural) memory is thought to reside in the limbic system, the amygdala, and the cerebellum.
Ref: Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 201 p. 64.
